title: Saber vs Conocer: Two Ways to Say “Know” in Spanish
seo_title: Saber vs Conocer: Two Ways to Say “Know” in Spanish
meta_description: Saber vs conocer: saber is knowing facts and how to do things, conocer is being familiar with people and places. Rules, examples, mistakes and a quiz.
excerpt: Knowing a fact or knowing a person? Spanish uses a different verb for each.

body_html:
Saber vs conocer is one of the first pairs learners meet, because English “know” covers both. The difference is the kind of knowledge. Saber is knowing information, facts and how to do something. Conocer is being familiar or acquainted with a person, a place or a thing through experience. Sé su número (I know her number) is information; La conozco (I know her) is acquaintance.

Quick answer
  • Saber = to know facts, information: Sé dónde vive.
  • Saber + infinitive = to know how to: Sé nadar.
  • Conocer = to know people, places, things by experience: Conozco Madrid.
  • In the preterite, conocer means “to meet”: La conocí en 2020.
{{toc}}

Saber vs conocer: the core rule

SaberConocer
Type of knowledgeFacts, information, skillsFamiliarity, acquaintance, experience
Typical objectsclauses (que, dónde, cuándo), infinitives, factspeople, places, works, products
ExampleSé que tienes razón. I know you’re right.Conozco a tu hermano. I know your brother.

The RAE dictionary defines conocer as having an idea of something or someone through the exercise of the intellect or experience, and saber as having knowledge or information about something.

When to use saber

  • Facts: ¿Sabes la respuesta? Do you know the answer?
  • With que, si and question words: No sé si viene. I don’t know if she’s coming. / ¿Sabes dónde está el baño?
  • Skills: Mi hijo sabe leer. My son can read. / ¿Sabes manejar? Can you drive?
  • By heart: Me sé la canción de memoria. I know the song by heart.
  • Finding out (preterite): Supe la noticia ayer. I found out the news yesterday.

Saber also means “to taste”: Esto sabe a limón (This tastes of lemon), ¡Qué bien sabe! (It tastes so good!).

When to use conocer

  • People: ¿Conoces a Laura? Do you know Laura? (personal a)
  • Places: No conozco México. I’ve never been to Mexico.
  • Works and things: ¿Conoces este libro? Are you familiar with this book?
  • Meeting someone (preterite): Nos conocimos en una boda. We met at a wedding.
  • Getting to know: Quiero conocerte mejor. I want to get to know you better.
{{image:2}}

The gray zone: subjects, languages, information

Some objects can take either verb with a slight change of nuance:

  • Sé mucho de historia (I know a lot about history) vs Conozco bien la historia de Perú (I’m very familiar with Peru’s history).
  • Sé francés (I know French, I can speak it) is common and natural; conozco el francés is rare.
  • Sé su dirección (I know the address, the information) vs Conozco la zona (I know the area, I’ve been there).

Ask yourself: could I have learned this from a text message? Then it’s saber. Did I need to experience it? Then it’s conocer.

{{book:the-mind-lies}}

Conjugation note

Saber is irregular: present sé, sabes, sabe (note the accent on sé, to distinguish it from se); preterite supe, supiste, supo; subjunctive sepa; future sabré. Conocer only changes in the first person present and the subjunctive: conozco, conozca.

Real conversations

At a party

  • A: ¿Conoces a ese chico? (Do you know that guy?)
  • B: No lo conozco, pero sé que es amigo de Marta. (I don’t know him, but I know he’s Marta’s friend.)
  • A: ¿Sabes cómo se llama? (Do you know his name?)
  • B: Ni idea. Vamos a conocerlo. (No idea. Let’s go and meet him.)

Travel plans

  • A: ¿Conoces Buenos Aires? (Have you been to Buenos Aires?)
  • B: Sí, la conozco bien. Sé dónde se come el mejor asado. (Yes, I know it well. I know where to eat the best barbecue.)

A quick mental shortcut

Think of conocer as “to be acquainted with” and saber as “to have the information”. You can know everything about a celebrity (sé mucho de ella) without ever having met her (no la conozco). That single sentence captures the whole difference.

One more pair of sentences to remember: Sé quién es (I know who he is) and Lo conozco (I know him personally). The first is information, the second a relationship.

Common mistakes

IncorrectCorrectWhy
Sé a María.Conozco a María.People: conocer
Conozco que es verdad.Sé que es verdad.Before que: saber
Sé cómo nadar.Sé nadar.Skills: saber + infinitive, no cómo
Conozco Juan.Conozco a Juan.Personal a
Se la respuesta.Sé la respuesta.Accent on sé (I know)
{{image:3}}

Try it yourself

  1. Do you know what time it is? (¿Sabes qué hora es?)
  2. I don’t know your parents. (No conozco a tus padres.)
  3. She can play the piano. (Sabe tocar el piano.)
  4. We met in Lima. (Nos conocimos en Lima.)
  5. I’ve never been to Spain. (No conozco España.)

Saber has its own tricky partner: see {{link:poder-vs-saber|poder vs saber}}. For every pair in the series, see {{link:spanish-confusing-words|my complete list of Spanish confusing words}}.

{{quiz}}

Final thoughts

Information and skills: saber. People, places and experience: conocer. Add the special preterite meanings (supe = I found out, conocí = I met) and you know, and understand, this pair.

faq.q: What is the difference between saber and conocer?
faq.a: Saber means to know facts, information or how to do something. Conocer means to know or be familiar with people, places and things through experience.

faq.q: How do you say “I know how to swim” in Spanish?
faq.a: Sé nadar. Saber + infinitive means to know how to do something; you don’t need cómo.

faq.q: What does conocer mean in the preterite?
faq.a: To meet for the first time: Conocí a mi pareja en la universidad (I met my partner at university).
